analogy.p: Imagine the atmosphere as a bath in which the water level is the amount of a particular gas. Volcanoes are the taps that pour in carbon dioxide and nitrogen. The oceans, algae and plants, and the formation of rocks and fossil fuels are plugholes that drain carbon dioxide out of the bath, while photosynthesis is a new tap that starts pouring oxygen in about 2.7 billion years ago. Nitrogen has no plughole, so it just builds up. The analogy breaks down because in a real atmosphere gases react with each other and the sizes of the flows changed enormously over time, whereas a bath has only simple steady flows.
analogy.t: A bath being filled and drained

bullets: The Earth is about **4.6 billion years old**, and the atmosphere has changed hugely over that time.
For about the **first billion years** there was **intense volcanic activity**.
The volcanoes released the gases that formed the **early atmosphere** and **water vapour** that later formed the **oceans**.
**Carbon dioxide** levels **fell**, while **oxygen** levels **rose** and **nitrogen** built up.
Today the main gases are about **80% nitrogen** and **20% oxygen** (exact figures: 78% and 21%).
The changes took **billions of years**, so the evidence is limited and the ideas are **theories**.
This topic links to **photosynthesis** (Biology), **fossil fuels** (4.7), **global warming** (4.9.2) and the **rock cycle**.
core.h: The big picture: how the atmosphere changed
core.p: The Earth's atmosphere today is about **80% nitrogen** and **20% oxygen**, with small proportions of other gases, but it has not always been this way. The specification asks you to know how scientists believe the **early atmosphere** formed, how it changed, and which processes made the atmosphere into the one that supports life today. The story has four main parts: **volcanoes** released gases and water vapour; the **oceans** formed and removed carbon dioxide; **algae and plants** used carbon dioxide and released **oxygen**; and carbon became **locked up** in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels. It is always described as a **theory**, because nobody was there to measure it.

bullets: Intense **volcanic activity** released gases, forming the early atmosphere.
The main gas was **carbon dioxide**.
There was **little or no oxygen** gas.
Volcanoes also gave out **nitrogen**, which gradually built up in the atmosphere.
There may have been **small proportions of methane and ammonia**.
Volcanoes also gave out **water vapour**, which was the source of water for the oceans.
Compare: the atmospheres of **Venus and Mars** today are mainly **carbon dioxide** (over 95%), which suggests the early Earth was similar.
Say 'may have been' in exam answers, because the early atmosphere is a **theory** based on limited evidence.
core.p: For roughly the first billion years of Earth's history the surface was extremely hot and unstable, with **intense volcanic activity**. Volcanoes released large amounts of gas from inside the Earth, and this outgassing formed the first atmosphere. The specification says that at the start of this period the atmosphere **may** have been like those of **Mars and Venus today**: mainly **carbon dioxide** with **little or no oxygen**. Volcanoes also released **nitrogen**, and there may have been small proportions of **methane** and **ammonia**. They released **water vapour** too, which was important for the next step.

bullets: The Earth **cooled** over time, so the water vapour **condensed** into liquid water.
Condensation is a **physical change** (gas to liquid).
The liquid water collected to form the **oceans**.
Oceans allowed **carbon dioxide to dissolve**, which removed it from the atmosphere.
Oceans also provided the habitat where **algae** first produced oxygen.
Written as a sequence: **volcanoes → water vapour → cooling → condensation → oceans**.
Do not say the water came from 'rain from space' or 'melting ice caps'; the specification says it came from **volcanic water vapour**.
core.p: As the Earth cooled, the **water vapour** that had been released by the volcanoes **condensed** to form liquid water. This water collected in hollows on the surface and formed the **oceans**. Forming oceans was a turning point, because carbon dioxide could now **dissolve** in the water, and ocean water allowed life, including the first algae, to develop. The key word that examiners want is **condensed**: water vapour is a gas, and cooling turns it to liquid water.

bullets: The atmospheres of **Venus and Mars** are mainly **carbon dioxide** (over 95%).
They contain **little or no oxygen**.
This supports the idea that the **early Earth** atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide.
The comparison works because those planets have **no photosynthesising life** to change the gases.
It is only **indirect evidence**: the planets differ in size, distance from the Sun and history.
Venus is much hotter, with a thick atmosphere; Mars has a thin one; Earth's today is very different.
Use the wording 'similar to the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today' in an answer.
core.p: Venus and Mars are the planets examiners use as a comparison. Both have atmospheres that are **mainly carbon dioxide**, with very little oxygen, and these atmospheres have **not** been changed by life. This supports the theory that the early Earth atmosphere was also mainly carbon dioxide. The comparison is useful because it is the closest thing to **evidence** we have: we can analyse the gases of other planets directly. However, the planets are different from the Earth in many ways, so the comparison is only an **analogy** and not proof.

bullets: It happened about **billions of years ago**, so there were **no direct observations** or measurements.
The **evidence is limited** because ancient rocks have been **changed or destroyed**.
Scientists use **indirect evidence**: rocks, trapped gases, other planets and computer models.
There are **different theories**, which is why the specification uses 'may have been'.
Theories are **tested and revised** as new evidence is found.
Peer review means other scientists check the **evidence and reasoning** before a theory is accepted.
A strong answer says why the evidence is limited, not just that it is.
core.h: Why theories about the early atmosphere are uncertain
core.p: The Earth's early atmosphere formed about **4 billion years ago**, so we cannot take direct samples. Scientists must use **indirect evidence**, such as the composition of very old rocks, gases trapped in rock bubbles, and the study of other planets. The evidence is limited because the rocks have been **changed, recycled or destroyed** over billions of years. This is why the specification says the evidence is **limited**, and why there are different theories about the early atmosphere. A good scientific theory is supported by evidence, can make predictions, and is **changed** if new evidence appears.

bullets: Nitrogen was released by **volcanoes**.
It is **unreactive**, so it did not take part in most chemical processes.
It is **not very soluble** in water, so the oceans did not remove much.
As other gases were removed, the **percentage of nitrogen** increased.
Nitrogen **built up gradually** over a very long time.
Today nitrogen is about **80%** (78%) of the atmosphere.
Link to bonding: the **triple bond** in the N₂ molecule makes it very stable and unreactive.
core.p: Nitrogen was released by volcanoes in small amounts, but it **gradually built up** in the atmosphere over hundreds of millions of years to become the most abundant gas. The reason is that **nitrogen is very unreactive**: it does not easily dissolve in the oceans, is not used up by photosynthesis, and does not take part in combustion at normal temperatures. Other gases such as carbon dioxide were removed by chemical and biological processes, but nitrogen stayed in the air, so its **proportion rose** until it became about 80% of the atmosphere.

bullets: Carbon dioxide **dissolved in the oceans** as they formed.
**Carbonates were precipitated**, forming sediments on the ocean floor.
Shells and skeletons of marine organisms (calcium carbonate) also formed sediments.
Sediments formed **sedimentary rocks** such as **limestone** (calcium carbonate).
This **reduced the amount of carbon dioxide** in the atmosphere.
The carbon in limestone is **locked up** and kept out of the atmosphere for millions of years.
Precipitation: a solid forming from a solution (for example, calcium ions plus carbonate ions form solid calcium carbonate).
core.h: Decreasing carbon dioxide (1): dissolving and carbonates
core.p: When the oceans formed, a large amount of **carbon dioxide dissolved in the water**. This reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. The dissolved carbon dioxide then reacted to form **carbonates**, which were **precipitated** (they formed solids that came out of solution) and settled on the sea floor as **sediments**. Marine organisms also used carbon and calcium to make **shells and skeletons** that were made of calcium carbonate. Over millions of years these deposits were compressed into **sedimentary rocks** such as **limestone**, which locked carbon away.

bullets: **Algae** first produced oxygen about **2.7 billion years ago**.
Plants soon after added to the oxygen in the atmosphere.
Algae and plants **use up carbon dioxide** in photosynthesis, so the percentage falls.
Word equation: **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen** (needs light, in chlorophyll).
Symbol equation: **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂**.
Photosynthesis is **endothermic** (it takes in energy from light).
Algae and plants produced the oxygen that now makes up about **20%** of the atmosphere.
Be ready to write the **balanced symbol equation** from memory.
core.h: Decreasing carbon dioxide (2): algae and plants, photosynthesis
core.p: About **2.7 billion years ago** **algae** first produced **oxygen**, and soon after this plants were adding oxygen to the atmosphere. Algae and plants **decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide** by taking it in for **photosynthesis**. In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water react using light energy absorbed by **chlorophyll** to make glucose and release oxygen. This is the process that changed the atmosphere from one with little oxygen into the oxygen-rich atmosphere we have today. It also makes the **base of nearly all food chains**.

bullets: **Coal** formed from **dead plants** buried over millions of years.
**Crude oil and natural gas** formed from **tiny marine organisms** under heat and pressure.
These **fossil fuels** are **hydrocarbons** and store carbon taken from the atmosphere by photosynthesis.
**Limestone** (sedimentary rock) stores carbon as calcium carbonate from shells and skeletons.
Locking away carbon **reduced** atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Burning fossil fuels today **releases** this carbon again (a link to global warming).
Fossil fuels are **finite, non-renewable** because they take millions of years to form.
core.h: Decreasing carbon dioxide (3): fossil fuels and sedimentary rocks
core.p: Much of the carbon that was once in the atmosphere as carbon dioxide is now stored in **sedimentary rocks** and **fossil fuels**. Algae and plants took in carbon dioxide and made carbon compounds. When these organisms died, some were buried and, over **millions of years**, the remains were changed by heat and pressure into **coal** (from plants) and **crude oil and natural gas** (from tiny marine organisms). The carbon in these fuels is **locked up** underground. Burning fossil fuels today releases it back into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, which is why carbon dioxide levels are rising now.

bullets: Before life, there was **little or no oxygen** in the atmosphere.
**Algae** produced oxygen from about **2.7 billion years ago**.
**Plants** then added more oxygen to the atmosphere.
Oxygen rose to about **20%** of the atmosphere.
Oxygen allowed the evolution of **organisms that respire aerobically**, including animals.
Rising oxygen was the **opposite** trend to the fall in carbon dioxide.
Link: aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic, which supports larger, more complex organisms.
core.p: Once photosynthesis began, oxygen was released faster than it was used up, so its **percentage rose** from almost zero to about **20%** over a very long period. This change was the most important event in the history of the atmosphere, because it allowed the evolution of **organisms that use oxygen for respiration**, including animals. The oxygen was produced first by algae in the oceans and then by plants on land. The rise was gradual, and the specification only requires you to state that **algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago** and that algae and plants produced the oxygen that makes up about 20% of the air.

bullets: Nitrogen: about **80%** (more exactly 78%).
Oxygen: about **20%** (more exactly 21%).
Argon, the most common **noble gas**: about **0.9%**.
Carbon dioxide: about **0.04%**.
**Water vapour** varies with weather and location.
Because the gases are not chemically combined, air is a **mixture** and not a compound.
Percentage by volume: to find the volume of oxygen in 250 cm³ of air, **20% × 250 = 50 cm³**.
Experiment: passing air over hot copper removes oxygen; the volume falls by about one-fifth.
core.p: The modern atmosphere is a **mixture of gases**. About **four-fifths (80%)** is **nitrogen** and about **one-fifth (20%)** is **oxygen**. The remaining small proportion contains various other gases, including **carbon dioxide**, **water vapour** and the **noble gases** (mainly argon). Carbon dioxide makes up only about **0.04%** of the air, but its effect on climate is large. The proportions are measured by volume, and the amount of water vapour varies from place to place and with the weather.

bullets: Check whether the x-axis is **'time ago'** (large numbers on the left) or time forward.
Describe a trend using **numbers** from the graph, for example 'fell from 95% to 0.04%'.
Explain the **fall in CO₂** using dissolving, photosynthesis and locking up in rocks or fuels.
Explain the **rise in O₂** using photosynthesis by algae and plants.
Explain the **rise in N₂ percentage** because it is unreactive and stays in the air.
Label the **time of key events**: algae at 2.7 billion years ago.
Do not confuse **percentage** with **amount**: a gas can rise in percentage when others fall.
core.h: Interpreting graphs and data about the atmosphere
core.p: Exam questions often give a graph of how the percentages of carbon dioxide and oxygen changed over time. The general trends to recognise are: **carbon dioxide high at the start and falling**, **oxygen near zero at the start and rising after about 2.7 billion years ago**, and **nitrogen gradually increasing** as other gases were removed. Read the axes carefully, as time may be shown as **'years ago'**, where the numbers decrease towards the present. When asked to explain a change, give a **named process** (dissolving, photosynthesis, formation of sedimentary rocks or fossil fuels) and link it to the gas.

bullets: For a 6-mark answer, follow **chronological order** and use all the key terms.
Use **processes**: condensation, dissolving, precipitation, photosynthesis.
Always state the **effect on each gas** (CO₂ down, O₂ up, N₂ up).
Write the **photosynthesis equation** if you are asked about oxygen production.
Mention **limited evidence** if asked why scientists disagree.
Link to **today**: burning fossil fuels reverses the carbon locking-up process.
Say **'about 20%'** and **'about 80%'** for oxygen and nitrogen unless asked for exact values.
core.h: Linking to other topics and exam technique
core.p: This topic connects strongly to other parts of the course. **Photosynthesis** appears in Biology, and the same equation is used. **Fossil fuels** and **combustion** link to Chemistry topic 4.7 and 4.9.2 (global warming), because burning fossil fuels returns the carbon that was locked up. **Sedimentary rocks** link to Geography and the carbonate chemistry of limestone. In the exam, 6-mark questions typically ask you to **describe and explain** how the atmosphere changed, so a well-organised answer follows the sequence: volcanoes, oceans, nitrogen, carbon dioxide decrease, oxygen increase.

exam: **State (1 mark):** give the percentages as 'about 80% nitrogen' and 'about 20% oxygen', and name carbon dioxide as a small proportion.
**Early atmosphere (2 marks):** 'volcanic activity released gases; mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen'; mention nitrogen, methane and ammonia for extra marks.
**Oceans (2 marks):** 'water vapour condensed as the Earth cooled'; 'formed the oceans'.
**Decrease in CO₂ (3 marks):** dissolved in the oceans; carbonates precipitated forming sediments; used by algae and plants in photosynthesis; locked in fossil fuels and sedimentary rocks.
**Rise in oxygen (2 marks):** 'algae (then plants) carried out photosynthesis' and 'released oxygen'.
**Equation (2 marks):** carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen; 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
**Why is the evidence limited? (2 marks):** the Earth is billions of years old, and the rocks have been changed or destroyed, so there are no direct records.
**6-mark 'describe how and why':** order your answer chronologically and cover volcanoes, oceans, nitrogen, CO₂ decrease (three ways) and oxygen rise.
**Graph questions:** quote values and times; state the trend; then explain using a named process.
**Calculation:** percentage = (volume of gas ÷ total volume) × 100; show working.
**Command words:** 'describe' = what happened; 'explain' = why it happened using a scientific process.

mistakes.r: The early atmosphere had little or no oxygen; oxygen came later from algae and plants (from about 2.7 billion years ago).
Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, soon followed by plants.
mistakes.w: 'Plants produced the first oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago.'

mistakes.r: Water vapour released by volcanoes condensed when the Earth cooled to form the oceans.
mistakes.w: 'The oceans formed from rain from space or ice.'

mistakes.r: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and releases oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
mistakes.w: 'Photosynthesis uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.'

mistakes.r: Nitrogen is unreactive, so it was not removed and its percentage built up in the atmosphere.
mistakes.w: 'Nitrogen decreased because it was used up.'

mistakes.r: It dissolved in the oceans, formed carbonate sediments and sedimentary rocks, was used in photosynthesis and became locked in fossil fuels.
It is a theory: evidence is limited because of the huge time scale.
mistakes.w: 'We know exactly what the early atmosphere was.'

mistakes.r: Coal formed from plants; crude oil and natural gas formed mainly from tiny marine organisms.

summary: You need to explain how the atmosphere formed from volcanic gases (mainly carbon dioxide, little or no oxygen, some nitrogen), how oceans formed by condensation, and how carbon dioxide fell and oxygen rose because of dissolving, carbonate sediments, photosynthesis by algae and plants and fossil fuel formation, giving today's atmosphere of about 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen. It matters because it explains why the atmosphere supports life and why burning fossil fuels changes it.

terms.d: The atmosphere formed by gases released from volcanoes during about the first billion years of the Earth's existence.
Eruptions that release gases such as carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water vapour from inside the Earth.
The change of state from gas to liquid, as when water vapour cooled to form the oceans.
A large body of liquid water formed when water vapour condensed as the Earth cooled.
A solid forming from a solution; carbonates were precipitated, forming sediments.
Solid material that settles on the bottom of a body of water, which can form sedimentary rock.
Rock, such as limestone, formed when sediments are compressed over millions of years.
A sedimentary rock made mostly of calcium carbonate, which locks up carbon.
The process by which algae and plants use carbon dioxide, water and light to make glucose and oxygen.
The green pigment in algae and plants that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
Simple aquatic organisms that first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago.
A fuel such as coal, crude oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms.
A compound containing hydrogen and carbon only; crude oil and natural gas are mostly hydrocarbons.
The unreactive Group 0 gases (for example argon) that make up a small part of the air.
An explanation supported by evidence that may be changed if new evidence appears.
Two or more substances that are not chemically combined, as in air.

worked.ans: Model answer: At first the atmosphere formed from gases released by intense volcanic activity and was mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen, and some nitrogen and possibly methane and ammonia. As the Earth cooled the water vapour condensed to form the oceans. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and carbonates were precipitated, forming sediments and sedimentary rocks, so the percentage of carbon dioxide fell. About 2.7 billion years ago algae began photosynthesis, and later plants did too; they removed carbon dioxide and released oxygen, so oxygen rose to about 20%. Carbon was also locked up in fossil fuels. Nitrogen, being unreactive, built up to about 80%.
worked.q: Describe how the Earth's atmosphere has changed from the early atmosphere to the atmosphere today and explain what caused the changes. (6 marks)
steps: Early atmosphere: intense volcanic activity released gases; mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen, probably some nitrogen, methane and ammonia, similar to Mars and Venus today.
Water vapour from the volcanoes condensed as the Earth cooled, forming the oceans.
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans, and carbonates were precipitated, forming sediments and sedimentary rocks, reducing carbon dioxide.
Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, soon followed by plants; photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) removed more carbon dioxide and increased oxygen.
Carbon was locked up in fossil fuels and limestone.
Nitrogen built up because it is unreactive.

worked.q: 100 cm³ of air is passed over heated copper until all the oxygen has reacted. The final volume of gas is 79 cm³. Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air. (2 marks)

worked.ans: It dissolved in the oceans, forming carbonate sediments; algae and plants removed it by photosynthesis; and carbon became locked up in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
worked.q: Explain why the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere decreased from over 95% to about 0.04%. (3 marks)
steps: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonates forming sediments.
Algae and plants used carbon dioxide in photosynthesis.
Carbon was locked in sedimentary rocks such as limestone and in fossil fuels.
